scenes.text: What if AI inference could become 1,000× faster using physics from the 1980s?
scenes.say: What if AI inference could become a thousand times faster, using physics from the nineteen eighties? That's the post. Here's the paper.

scenes.headline: CRAM: a Hopfield-Tank energy that learns
scenes.sub: What is minimised, how it reasons, and what the 1,000× measures
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Merrow! CRAM takes an energy from nineteen eighty-five, learns its costs from solved puzzles, and reasons by rolling downhill.

scenes.credit: Prefrontal's animation, from @crazyMLguy's post on X

steps.say: Clamp the clues of a Sudoku. Fill every other cell at random. Now walk downhill on an energy.

steps.caption: Several chains, one stopping threshold
steps.say: When any chain's energy falls below a threshold fitted from the training solutions, the search stops.

scenes.title: One unit of energy per clash

legend: Every link: two peers holding the same digit
Plain descent: stuck with clashes left
A little temperature, and it climbs out

steps.term: Energy: one unit per clashing pair
steps.say: Here is the energy, hand-set. Every pair of cells in the same row, column or box that holds the same digit costs one unit.
Move one cell at a time to its cheapest digit, and the board parks in a valley with clashes left. No single change helps.

steps.term: Focused Gibbs: redraw a clashing cell at random
steps.say: So shake it. Pick a clashing cell, redraw its digit with a little temperature. Sometimes the energy goes up. Then it finds the floor.
A valid board has energy zero, so the search knows when it is done.

scenes.credit: Prefrontal's animation, from @crazyMLguy's post on X

steps.say: Training learns the costs. Pull down the energy of each solved board.
Push up the boards one cell away. No search is unrolled, so nothing is backpropagated through time.

steps.caption: 48 ms with pseudolikelihood
steps.say: Same energy, different objectives. Pseudolikelihood reaches ninety-nine percent in forty-eight milliseconds.

steps.caption: One-step BPTT: 4.4 s
steps.say: Backprop through one step takes four point four seconds. Full backprop through time never gets there.

scenes.label: Sudoku constraint pairs, found in every checkpoint
scenes.say: The learned weights are the rules. Positive costs on exactly the eight hundred and ten pairs of cells that share a row, column or box. My own laptop fit found the same.

steps.say: These are training times, on one H two hundred. Sudoku trains about a hundred thousand times faster than the quickest baseline.
The thousand comes from one row: N-Queens, against HRM.

steps.term: Warm fit: start-up costs already paid
steps.say: And CRAM is timed warm. Charge it the start-up the baselines pay, and that row lands right around a thousand.

right.title: The paper
right.say: The paper measures training time, and inference in counted operations, not seconds. No special hardware anywhere.

steps.caption: Hand-set: one weight, every Sudoku solved
steps.say: Then the authors set the weights by hand. One number solves every Sudoku in the test set.
Three solve every maze. A perfect score on these benchmarks shows a few pairwise rules, nothing more.

scenes.text: The speed is real and the benchmarks are too easy. CRAM proves both at once.
scenes.say: The speed is real, and the benchmarks are too easy. CRAM proves both at once.
An old energy, learned in milliseconds, and a warning about Sudoku. Thanks for watching!
